summary: This standards-track document defines an abstract base YANG data model for network and service topologies and inventories. More specific models for particular technologies are expected to extend it. It gives a common vocabulary for describing nodes, links and how they connect.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC gives network devices and controllers a shared way to write down what a network looks like: which networks exist, what sits in them, and how the parts are joined. Other, more specific models add the details of a particular technology on top of that common base.

questions: what is the yang data model for network topologies
how to describe a network topology in yang
how to model network topology in yang
what is a termination point in network topology
subtitle: A common YANG vocabulary for describing networks, nodes and links.

tldr.problem: Every network technology describes its own topology in its own way, so an application that wants a general view of the network, including how layers sit on top of each other, has nothing common to read.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two YANG modules, ietf-network and ietf-network-topology, which model networks, the nodes they contain, the links between them and the termination points that anchor those links, and which allow a network to refer to the network below it.
tldr.outcome: More specific models, such as the Layer 3 topology model, add their own detail by augmenting the base model, so that data stays in one consistent shape while a controller can compare its view with the devices' own view.

today: RFC 8345 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its text names RFC 8346 (Layer 3 topologies) as an example of a model that extends it.

sections.title: What the Base Model Covers
sections.content:
The document introduces an abstract, or base, YANG data model to represent networks and topologies, and it is split into two parts. The first defines a network data model that enables network hierarchies, meaning networks layered on top of each other, and maintains an inventory of the nodes in a network. The second augments that model with topology information: it adds the concepts of links and termination points to describe how nodes in a network are connected to one another, and it introduces vertical layering relationships between networks that can be augmented to cover both network inventories and network or service topologies.

The two parts could have been combined into a single model, but the separation makes integration easier, because inventory information can be augmented separately from topology.

The model is generic, so it can be applied to many kinds of network and service topology. Technology-specific models add the specifics, for example a model for Layer 2 topologies, for Layer 3 topologies such as unicast IGP, IS-IS and OSPF, for traffic engineering data, or for transport and service topologies. An application can then work with an inventory or topology of any network at a generic level, where the details of a particular type are not needed, while the instantiated data still follows the same structure when a model is augmented.

The abstract network module, ietf-network, holds a list of abstract network nodes and defines the network hierarchy or stack, where a network may have one or more supporting networks. The network topology module, ietf-network-topology, defines a topology graph and the components it is made of: nodes, edges and termination points. Nodes represent graph vertices, links represent graph edges, and nodes contain the termination points that anchor the links. A network may hold several topologies, for example topologies at different layers and overlay topologies, so the model allows relationships between topologies as well as dependencies between nodes and termination points across them.
sections.plainLanguage: The base model says three things: a network exists, it contains nodes, and nodes are joined by links that end at ports. Specific models then say what kind of network it is and what the ports really are.

sections.title: Networks, Nodes and the Underlay Stack
sections.content:
The base network model has a container holding a list of networks, and each network is a separate list entry distinguished by a network-id. A network has one or more types, such as L2, L3, OSPF or IS-IS, captured under the container network-types, which in this model serves only as an augmentation target: network-specific modules later insert a node for each type below it. Network types SHOULD always be represented with presence containers rather than empty leaves, so that hierarchies of network subtypes can be represented, such as an OSPF network which is at the same time a Layer 3 unicast IGP network.

A network can be part of a hierarchy of networks built on top of other networks, and those are captured in the list supporting-network. A supporting network is, in effect, an underlay network.

A network also contains an inventory of its nodes, each identified relative to its containing network by a node-id. A node does not exist independently of a network: it is part of the network that holds it. Where the same device takes part in several networks or at several layers, it is represented by several nodes, one for each network, because a node is an abstraction of the device for that particular network. To show that one entity belongs to several topologies, one can create a physical network with a list of nodes for each device, and refer to that network as the underlay of the logical networks above it. The model allows more than one underlay, so layered topologies and service topologies can sit alongside their physical instantiation.

Nodes can in turn be supported by other nodes and map onto one or more nodes in an underlay network, which the list supporting-node captures. That hierarchy of nodes also represents device stacks, where a node at one level is supported by a set of nodes at the level below, such as a router node supported by a node for a route processor and nodes for line cards and service modules.
sections.plainLanguage: A node belongs to one network, so a device that appears in three layers is written down as three nodes. Pointing one node at another is how the model records that the upper layer sits on the lower one.

sections.title: Links and Termination Points
sections.content:
The topology model augments the network model with links, which say how nodes are connected, and termination points, which anchor those links and live inside the nodes. A termination point might be a physical or logical port, or more generally an interface. Like a node, a termination point can be supported by an underlying termination point contained in the supporting node of the underlay network.

A link is identified by a link-id that is unique within a given topology. Links are point-to-point and unidirectional, so each link has a source and a destination, and both refer to a node and to a termination point on that node. As with a node, a link can map onto one or more links in an underlay topology, and that mapping is captured in the list supporting-link.

Links are terminated by a single termination point, not a set of them. Connections that involve multihoming or link aggregation therefore have to be written as several point-to-point links, with a link at a higher layer that is supported by those individual links. Similarly, a bidirectional connection is a pair of unidirectional links, and a multipoint network can be written with pseudonodes, much as IS-IS does it, with new links introduced at that level for the non-point-to-point patterns.
sections.plainLanguage: Every link runs from one port on one node to one port on another node, in one direction. Anything more complicated, such as a bundle of links or a two-way connection, is built out of those simple links.

sections.title: How Technology-Specific Models Extend It
sections.content:
To derive a data model for a specific type of network, the base model is extended by a new YANG module that defines augmentations against ietf-network and ietf-network-topology.

The augmentations against ietf-network come first. A new network type is defined as a presence container, inserted by augmentation below the network-types container. Data nodes for node parameters specific to that network type are then defined and augmented into the node list, and they can be made conditional on the presence of the corresponding network type in the containing network with a when statement. Where there are requirements about network hierarchies, such as a network type that requires a particular kind of underlay network, corresponding constraints can be defined and the supporting-network list augmented accordingly, though care should be taken not to over-define constraints.

Augmentations against ietf-network-topology follow, defining data nodes for link parameters and for termination point parameters specific to the new network type, inserted into the link and termination point lists respectively, again possibly conditional on the network type.

It is possible, but not required, to group the data nodes for a network type under a dedicated container. That introduces more structure but lengthens the data node path names. Where a hierarchy of network types is defined, augmentations can also be applied against augmenting modules, so that the module of a more specific network type augments the module of a more general one.
sections.plainLanguage: Another model adds its own detail by inserting new fields into the places this model leaves open: a container for the network type, and fields for its nodes, links and ports.

sections.title: The Design Decisions Behind the Model
sections.content:
Several choices shape the model. The containment structure is kept relatively flat: the lists of nodes, links, termination points and the supporting lists are not kept in separate containers, so path identifiers that refer to a specific node stay compact. The trade-off is that there is no separate structure in the instance data separating elements of different lists, which is not semantically required but might help human readability in some cases.

Mappings between networks, nodes, links and termination points are kept strictly generic, to avoid assumptions about what an entity really represents. The model does not say whether a termination point is an interface or whether a node is a particular device. Where more specifics are needed, an augmenting module adds them, for example a leaf of type interface-ref on a termination point or a leaf referring to a network element on a node.

A network can churn while other networks are layered on top of it, so deleting a supporting node, link or termination point leaves references dangling in the overlay. The model uses the require-instance construct of YANG 1.1 for this. A dangling reference leaves the instance without referential integrity, so it is removed from the operational state datastore and appears only in the intended datastore until the situation is resolved, either by adding the supporting object or by reconfiguring the instance to refer to something that exists. The application maintaining the overlay is responsible for this; when a server receives a request to configure an overlay network, it SHOULD check that the supporting objects really exist in the operational state datastore, and requests that refer to objects that do not exist SHOULD be rejected.

The model uses groupings rather than defining data nodes inline, which makes it easier to include the same nodes in notifications, at the cost of more complex constraints. Links are point-to-point and unidirectional, which keeps the model simple and generic and makes it easy to use with graph algorithms. Network types are represented with a container of presence containers rather than an empty leaf or a leaf-list, so that network types can refine one another.

Identifiers of nodes, networks, links and termination points are URIs rather than plain strings. Strings would be easier to implement and easier for people, but the structure of a string has to be agreed with every system that works with the data, whereas a URI makes the structure explicit, can be fed into a URI resolver, and can be correlated across systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The model is deliberately plain: no assumptions about what a node or a port really is, one-direction links, and identifiers that are web addresses so that the same object can be recognised across systems.

sections.title: Configured Topologies and Discovered Ones
sections.content:
YANG requires a data node to be either configuration data or operational data, but not both, while it is important to have all network information, including cross-network dependencies, in one coherent model. In most cases the topology of a network is discovered, but certain topologies, such as overlay topologies, must also be configurable by an application.

The model therefore designates all data as configuration data, and the distinction between what is configured and what is in effect comes from the datastores of the Network Management Datastore Architecture. Discovered topology is populated automatically in the operational state datastore, where it is system controlled. Configured topology is instantiated in a configuration datastore, such as the intended datastore, and only when it has actually taken effect is it also instantiated in the operational state datastore.

For each network, the origin of its data is given by the origin metadata annotation: discovered data is learned and configured data is intended. A configured topology refers to an underlay topology and includes layering information, such as the supporting nodes underlying a node, the supporting links underlying a link and the supporting termination points underlying a termination point. The supporting objects must be instantiated in the operational state datastore for the dependent overlay object to be reflected there; if a configured item has a dangling reference, it is removed from the operational datastore and shows up only in the intended one, and it is up to the client application to fix the reference.
sections.plainLanguage: The same model holds both what the network discovered and what an operator configured. Which datastore the data sits in says which one it is, and an overlay is only live once the things it rests on really exist.

sections.title: The Registered Modules and Namespaces
sections.content:
The document registers four namespace URIs in the IETF XML Registry, each with the IESG as registrant contact: urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-network, urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-network-topology, urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-network-state and urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-network-topology-state.

Four YANG module names are registered in the YANG Module Names registry. The module ietf-network has the prefix nw and the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-network. The module ietf-network-topology has the prefix nt and the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-network-topology. The two companion modules for implementations that do not support the Network Management Datastore Architecture are ietf-network-state, with the prefix nw-s, and ietf-network-topology-state, with the prefix nt-s. All four refer to RFC 8345.
sections.plainLanguage: The module names and their namespaces are recorded so that any implementation can refer to the same data and be sure it means the same thing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The modules are meant to be reached through management protocols such as NETCONF or RESTCONF. The lowest NETCONF layer is the secure transport layer, where Secure Shell is mandatory to implement, and the lowest RESTCONF layer is HTTPS, where TLS is mandatory to implement. The NETCONF access control model provides the means to restrict a given user's access to a preconfigured subset of the available operations and content.

The network topology and inventory created by these modules reveal the structure of the network, which could be very helpful to an attacker. Although no personally identifiable information is defined in the modules, node identifiers may be associated with devices that are in turn associated with specific users.

Some of the data is writable, for example in the case of overlay topologies created by client applications, so a malicious client could introduce topologies that are undesired, or add or remove a node, a link or a termination point. For a learned topology the server automatically refuses such attempts, but for a configured topology, whose origin is intended, the change could take effect and be reflected in the operational state datastore, which would disrupt the services carried over that topology. The topology could be cut or configured in a suboptimal way, wasting underlay resources, and service levels could degrade or fail. That is why the NETCONF access control model should be applied vigorously to prevent topology misconfiguration by unauthorized clients.
sections.plainLanguage: A topology map is useful to an attacker, and a client that is allowed to edit one could break the network by cutting links. Access control therefore matters here more than usual.

items.title: Flat containment
items.text: Lists are not split into separate containers, so paths to a node stay compact.

items.title: Generic mappings
items.text: The model does not assume a node is a device or a port is an interface.

items.title: One-direction links
items.text: Links are point-to-point and unidirectional, which suits graph algorithms.

items.title: URI identifiers
items.text: Identifiers are URIs, so the same object can be recognised across systems.

items.title: Presence containers
items.text: Network types use presence containers so one type can refine another.

items.title: Churn handling
